en: A pesky countergambit: sacrifice e5 to plant a pawn on d4, a permanent thorn in White's camp, and attack fast. Dubious deep down, but biting and full of traps.
Main — 3.dxe5 d4 4.Nf3
Lasker Trap — 4.e3??
If White doesn't play c4
The London. No c4, so no Albin: …e5 would no longer be a gambit but a pawn given away.
The Albin Countergambit: offer e5 to push …d4 and seize the initiative.
The d4 pawn is the heart of the Albin: advanced and protected, it cramps White's whole development.
The natural move… but losing: opening with e3 walks into the famous Lasker Trap.
White prepares b4 for space; …a5 freezes the queenside and keeps good play.
The second mistake, the fatal one: recapturing the bishop lets the e3 pawn run. fxe3 was forced.
The pawn races on: check, and the underpromotion follows.
UNDERPROMOTION to a knight with check! (A queen would allow Rxg1.) Black wins material — the Lasker Trap.
The same spirit as the countergambit — hit d4 without delay — but with a sound move.
We pin the defender of d4. That's the method against every system that builds this pawn without supporting it with c3 in time.
Provocative: the knight invites White's pawns forward… to turn them into targets. A venomous hypermodern weapon.

A third of games. White declines to push e5 and therefore to play the Alekhine at all: no knight chased, no counterattack.
White chases the knight straight away…
The sound modern line: White settles for a reasonable centre.
White grabs all the space…
Pin the f3-knight, defender of d4 and e5.
The fianchetto: the g7 bishop will bite on White's centre and the e5 square.
The knight retreats; Black will target the centre with …d5 or …dxe5.
The Four Pawns Attack: impressive, but those pawns become targets after …dxe5 and …c5.
The exchange: quiet play where Black ends up well developed and solid.
The chase: the pawn pushes again. The knight finds shelter and the c5-pawn will be weak.
The reply that restores play: we hit e4 in the centre rather than endure a quiet development.
White's doubled pawns against a broad centre: we hit d4 at once — the lasting weakness of this structure.
Three Black players in five play this here, and the chapter went elsewhere. Strike the centre BEFORE it solidifies.
White stops …Bg4. Without that precaution, the pin would make d4 indefensible.
Most club opponents dodge the Open Sicilian. Here are sound answers to the Alapin, Rossolimo, Grand Prix, Smith-Morra and friends.

Rossolimo — 3.Bb5
The Alapin: White prepares d4 without allowing …cxd4 tricks. Striking the centre is the key.
The Smith-Morra Gambit: a pawn for fast development and open files.
The Wing Gambit: a flank pawn to deflect the c-pawn and grab the centre.
Seen in one club game in eight: White develops the bishop first. Playable, but toothless.
The simplest reply: open up and equalise cleanly.
The other main reply: hit e4 immediately.
White gains a tempo on the queen by pushing d4.
Both sides develop; a balanced isolated queen's-pawn (IQP) structure arises.
The pawn advances; the knight must go to d5, where it gets harassed.
The bishop hits the d5-knight; Black kicks it and strikes at e5.
A common move order that keeps every option open.
The Rossolimo: White trades on c6 to play the structure. …g6 is reliable.

The OPEN Sicilian, played nearly half the time — and this course is not about it: it covers the anti-Sicilians. What follows keeps you afloat, it is not a treatment. The Open Sicilian is a repertoire of its own.
One White player in five puts the bishop on c4, and the course only planned for the Rossolimo 3.Bb5. The bishop eyes f7 but bothers little: we are going to make it a target.
The Alapin by transposition: White prepares d4 without ever allowing …cxd4 and Nxd4. The course did not see it coming in this order.
Keep the structure intact and chase the bishop with …a6/…b5.
With queens likely to come off, Black's bishop pair offsets the doubled pawn.
Nearly one White player in two trades here, and the course only planned for castling. They hand us the bishop pair in exchange for doubled pawns.
The Moscow: the b5 check. …Bd7 is clean and trouble-free.
White declines the sidelines and enters the Open Sicilian: this course stops here. What follows belongs to the Dragon, Najdorf and Scheveningen courses.
The same bishop, against our …d6 move order. The course only knew 3.Bb5+ and 3.d4.
The combative version: keep the light bishop for …e5 and …Be7.
Accept, then defend precisely to neutralise the gambit.
The bishop eyes f7; Black adopts the standard defensive setup.
Against the pressure on e5/d5, the …a6, …Nf6, …Be7, …0-0 formation holds firm.
The queen BEFORE the bishop: …Be7 at once allows e5! and White gets everything back with interest.
The Grand Prix: White wants f4-f5 and a kingside assault. …g6 and …Bg7 contain it.
The Closed: a manoeuvring game. Black grabs queenside space with …Rb8 and …b5.
The bishop comes to pin/trade on c6 to weaken Black's grip on the centre.
The clean refutation: give the pawn back to open the centre and seize the initiative.
The starting point of the whole Open Sicilian. If you play the Sicilian seriously, this is the junction to study next.
The positional refutation: …e6 prepares …d5 and the c4 bishop will have to move a second time.
The bishop is already relocating — two tempi gone. Black equalises without effort.
The Sveshnikov: we kick the d4 knight at once and accept the d5 hole in exchange for very active piece play. The easiest line to remember for someone coming from the anti-Sicilians.
We hit e4 at once. If White pushes e5, that pawn will be weak and our knight will find good squares.
The position opens and we are the ones who benefit: the advanced e5 pawn is gone, and the c4 bishop faces a wall of black pawns.
The Najdorf move, doubly useful here: it prepares …b5, which will chase the c4 bishop off its diagonal with tempo.
The principled answer: we strike in the centre before White's big centre exists. Against the Alapin, waiting is always a mistake.
We trade queens deliberately: without them, the advanced c5 pawn stops being an asset and becomes a weakness to collect at leisure.
We recapture with the b-pawn, not the d-pawn: the b-file opens for our rook, and the c6 pawn will support …d5 when the time comes.
White prepares d4 to open up before our bishops breathe. That is the race in this structure: our two bishops against their better pawn structure.
A pawn sacrificed for permanent queenside pressure: open a- and b-files, the g7 bishop on the long diagonal. The compensation lasts into the endgame.

The London. The Benko assumes 2.c4 c5 3.d5 b5: with no c4 pawn there is nothing to undermine, and the sacrifice loses its point.
White delays c4. We develop without committing: if c4 comes later, the Benko is back on.
White pushes; Black will undermine the c4/d5 base with …b5.
The Benko Gambit: offering b5 to open the a- and b-files.
Declining by developing: Black takes on c4 and keeps a comfortable game.
White tries to freeze the queenside. …b4 keeps space and good play.
The a6 bishop hampers White's f1 bishop: that's the essence of the gambit.
White keeps the f1 bishop by grabbing the centre: the king must walk by hand.
We trade White's good bishop. No gambit available, so we play the structure — and that's the right way to meet the London.
The knight takes its outpost. We answer …O-O then …c5, and the game becomes an ordinary structural fight.
1.f4: a Dutch with White, a tempo up. Control e5, fianchetto or set up a Stonewall, then attack the enemy king.
Classical — reversed Dutch
From's Gambit — 1…e5

vs …d5 — the classical Bird
Grab control of e5 at once: it's a Dutch a tempo up.
From's Gambit: a pawn for attack. The right path is to return the pawn and end up well placed.
More than a quarter of games, and the chapter didn't mention it. Black prepares …Bg4 and …e5.
Black plays a reversed Dutch in turn. The game becomes a battle of plans, not theory.
Black shuts the diagonal first. The course saw …Nf6, …Nc6 and …c5, but not this perfectly natural move.
The good bishop out before …e6 — the golden rule, which Black applies here against us.
The modern version of the gambit: instead of …d6 at once, Black develops and keeps the threat alive.
One Black player in three pins at once — the most frequent move in the From's Gambit, and the course only knew …g5. The f3 knight guards h4 and g5: pinning it prepares …Qh4+.
Quiet development instead of a pin. One Black player in five, and the course said nothing about it.
The bishop comes out before …e6 so as not to be shut in — good method, but it hands us a tempo.
We hit the defender of e5: the sore point of every Black setup against the Bird.
Doubled pawns, and the e5 square is ours for good.
Give the pawn back at the right moment rather than clinging to it: that's the classic mistake against From's.
Nearly three Black players in four develop this knight here, and the course only planned for …a6.
Double fianchetto against classical development: we'll play Nh4 to trade that bishop, our opponent's best piece.
Modest and sufficient: we open the f1 bishop to castle quickly. Against a gambit, finishing development beats trying to refute.
Black keeps the bishop for the attack. We have the extra pawn and a safe king: precisely the gambit's bargain, and it suits us.
The jump that hits e3: Black tries to win the pawn back with checks. You need to know what follows — it is forced.
And here is the point: we offer the queen trade. Without queens the gambit's attack no longer exists, and our d4 centre stays on the board.
The pin used the other way round: we deliberately trade our good bishop to weaken Black's grip on e5 — the square the whole Bird revolves around.
The knight settles on the outpost, and no minor piece can evict it any more. That is the point of everything before it.
The “Larsen” Bird: the queen's bishop goes to b2, eyeing e5 and the long diagonal. Our two slowest pieces then aim at the same square.
We fianchetto on our side: the g2 bishop will contest f5 on the light squares, and it is the only way not to hand over that diagonal.
Black pushes on the kingside since the centre is blocked. We answer h3: the h5 pawn goes no further without conceding something.
The bishop hits c4 on move two, eyeing f7 without committing the king's knight. Often a rerouted Italian, with the option of a d4 centre or quiet play with d3.

Quiet line — 4.d3
The Italian bishop without …Nf3: keeping the choice between quiet d3 and sharp d4.
A third of games, and the course started from …Nf6 or …Bc5. The most natural move was untreated.
A modest reply — one player in ten — the course ignored: it only saw …Nf6, …Bc5 and …Nc6. Black shuts the c4 bishop's diagonal with a pawn.
The Urusov Gambit: a pawn for lightning development and an attack on f7.
Over a third of games after 3.d3, and the chapter went elsewhere. A symmetrical position and slow play: plans decide.
One Black player in five develops like this, and the course only saw …c6 and …Bc5.
Preparing d4 to build a centre: the spirit of the Evans Gambit, without …b4.
One Black player in five takes the e4 pawn rather than d4 — an inaccuracy the course did not flag. The knight ends up alone in enemy territory.
We transpose into the Italian, and it is the most frequent case — one Black player in three. The course only planned for …Nf6.
The waiting move that develops nothing. One Black player in seven plays it, and it is paid for in cash.
We switch into the Two Knights, the sharpest line: f7 is hit twice.
The right defence. Recapturing on d5 would lose to Nxf7 — the trap every 3.Ng5 player is hoping for.
Black pins before we get Nbd2 in. We answer Bg5: the pin cuts both ways.
King to safety first. In these quiet positions, whoever castles first then decides where the game will be played.
The knight goes after the c5 bishop, Black's best piece. Trading it is worth the trip, even round the edge of the board.
Since they play small, we take big: Black has spent two moves contesting nothing in the centre.
We open the d-file and evict the knight with a pawn. White is clearly better: the quiet punishment of …Nxe4.
The slow Italian structure: we prepare d4 step by step, and the c5 bishop will one day have to choose between retreating and trading.
Black recaptures with the KING: no more castling, and an endgame where the tempo spent on …h6 counts twice.
A pawn for instant attack: an open f-file, fast development and the enemy king in the crosshairs. The attacker's weapon against 1…d5.

Black accepts; White will grab the initiative back with f3.
The most common decline — one player in ten — and the course only planned for the capture …dxe4. They steer into a French, where our gambit no longer exists.
Black develops the bishop before returning the pawn. One player in eight, and the course only saw …Nf6.
The countergambit: Black cements e4 with a pawn instead of returning it. One player in eight, missing from the course — and the line where improvising costs the most.
The Ryder Gambit: a SECOND pawn sacrificed for immediate attack. Objectively dubious, fearsome in practice — and the course said nothing about it.
Black develops the bishop before …e6. White chases it with Ne5 and g4.
The most played defence against the gambit — nearly one game in two — and the only one the course didn't cover. Black pins the knight guarding d4.
Nearly three Black players in ten shut the diagonal rather than develop a bishop, and the course only planned for …g6, …Bf5 and …Bg4. It is the soundest defence to the gambit.
The key manoeuvre: the queen swings to h4 to attack the king with Bh6 and Ne5.
Black plugs d5 and holds. The pawn does not come back here: the gambit is played for the initiative, not to be materially level.

The real test, and it must be said plainly: this pin gives Black the advantage back (≈ +0.7). The course used to teach 8…h6 here, which loses — learning an attack against the wrong defence means learning to lose against the right one.
